survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study merged PIAAC Round 1 public-use files across 22 participating countries to form a pooled analytic dataset of adult respondents. For country-level estimates of disengagement, the authors first computed person-level disengagement by averaging dichotomous disengaged indicators across items within each domain, and then averaged these person-level values to obtain population means. In this second aggregation step, they explicitly used sampling weights to account for the selection procedure and sample composition, and they used replicate weights to quantify uncertainty of the population estimates. The paper also notes that descriptive proportions in some earlier tables (e.g., Table 3) are unweighted, so weighted interpretation is primarily for the country-difference analyses and subgroup comparisons.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper uses plausible values for assigning respondents to PIAAC competence score groups (it states that the first plausible value was used), but it does not describe any missing-data handling strategy for the analytic variables used to derive disengagement indicators and subgroup comparisons. Missingness is mentioned for age (with a share of cases having missing age information), yet the methodology does not specify whether cases with missing background variables were excluded or imputed. This is therefore a reporting gap for missing-data treatment in the disengagement indicator analyses.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study used PIAAC Round 1 public-use files downloaded from the OECD website (18 July 2014) and merged all countries that participated in the PIAAC main study, yielding 152,514 participants from 22 countries. It excluded data from two additional countries (Australia and Cyprus) because they were not published in the public-use files. For the country-level disengagement plots and comparisons, it further restricted to respondents who did not opt out of the computer-based assessment (explicitly stated for Figures 13–15). For educational-attainment subgroup analyses, it restricted to respondents aged 25–65 (to assume completed schooling). For language subgroup analyses, it notes that the public-use file lacked valid language information for the Russian Federation, so language results are not reported for RUS.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD study develops and validates empirical indicators of test-taking engagement in PIAAC by classifying item responses as engaged vs. disengaged using response-time thresholds. It compares two constant thresholds (3000 ms and 5000 ms) with two item-specific approaches: visual inspection of bimodal response-time distributions (VI) and a proportion-correct conditional threshold (P+>0%), where the threshold is the shortest response time associated with proportion correct greater than zero. Validity checks show that P+>0% performs slightly better than VI and constant-threshold methods, with disengaged responses exhibiting near-zero success rates. Using the P+>0% method, disengagement is low in Literacy (generally <5% of responses) and extremely low in Numeracy (often <1%), while Problem solving shows higher disengagement (typically >5% but usually <10%). Country differences are statistically significant with small-to-medium effect sizes, disengagement is highly correlated across domains, and disengagement is negatively associated with proficiency; subgroup differences by gender, age, education, and language are mostly insignificant or very small. The paper emphasizes that the design does not support causal inference and that disengagement detection based on short response times may miss disengaged behavior with long response times.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD technical study focused on defining and validating behavioral indicators (response-time thresholds) and describing descriptive and correlational group/country differences in disengagement. It does not train or evaluate machine-learning predictive models, so ML technique fields are intentionally empty and no predictive main findings are reported. Some metadata (e.g., author list and publication year) are not present in the provided text excerpt, so they are left as null rather than inferred.
